tool.name: TopographicWetnessIndex
tool.summary: Computes the Topographic Wetness Index (TWI), also called the Compound Topographic Index (CTI): the natural log of the specific catchment area divided by the local slope gradient. High values mark cells with a large upslope contributing area and/or a gentle slope -- valley bottoms and convergence zones prone to wetness -- while low values mark ridges and steep, diverging slopes. Sink filling, flow direction (D8, MFD or D-Infinity, your choice) and flow accumulation are computed internally (no Spatial Analyst extension required), or you may supply a pre-filled DEM and/or a flow-accumulation raster.
tool.usage:
The Topographic Wetness Index (Beven and Kirkby 1979) combines two things that control where water collects: the size of the area draining to a cell, and the slope at that cell. It is defined as TWI = ln( a / tan(beta) ), where a is the specific catchment area and tan(beta) is the local slope gradient (rise over run). TWI is high where a large area drains through a gentle slope (water arrives and lingers -- valley bottoms, hollows, flats) and low on steep ridges that shed water. It is a purely topographic estimate of relative wetness: it captures the shape of the land, not rainfall, soils, or subsurface flow, and Beven and Kirkby themselves framed it as a model for humid temperate areas, so in arid regions it describes drainage geometry more than actual soil moisture.
Specific catchment area and the unit contour length. The specific catchment area is the upslope contributing area divided by the length of the contour (the width of flow) across which that water passes -- it standardizes catchment area by the outlet width, so its units are area per unit length (square meters of catchment per meter of outlet). In a raster every cell is treated as its own outlet, so the unit contour length is simply the cell size. Because the catchment area of a cell is (its upslope cell count) times the cell area, and the cell area is the cell size squared, dividing by the unit contour length (one cell size) leaves: specific catchment area = (flow accumulation + 1) x cell size. The +1 counts the cell's own catchment (a cell always drains at least itself), which also keeps the value above zero so the logarithm is defined. This tool divides catchment area by the unit contour length, giving the properly standardized specific catchment area; a common shortcut instead multiplies flow accumulation by the cell area and omits that division, which only shifts every value by a constant amount (the spatial pattern is identical) but is not the standardized form.
The slope term and epsilon. On a perfectly flat cell tan(beta) is zero, which would divide by zero, so a small constant (the "Value added to slope" parameter, default 0.0001) is added to the slope gradient; a flat cell then receives a high (very wet) value, as intended. Slope is computed from the original, unfilled DEM (Horn's method), because the DEM is filled only to keep flow routing from getting stuck in sinks -- for the slope itself the true, unmodified surface is wanted.
How the hydrology is computed. Everything is done internally with no Spatial Analyst dependency, so the tool runs anywhere ArcGIS Pro's Python is installed. Sinks are removed by the priority-flood algorithm (Barnes, Lehman and Mulla 2014); flow is routed across the filled surface by the method you choose (below); flats drain to the nearest exit; and flow accumulation is the upslope area draining to each cell, in cells. The fill is identical to Esri's Fill tool. On a projected floating-point DEM the D8 accumulation matches Esri's on more than 99.8 percent of cells and D-Infinity on more than 99.7 percent (the remainder is tie-breaking on flats); MFD agrees within 5 percent on about 83 percent of cells, because Esri's MFD implementation is not fully documented. On an integer DEM, where neighbors often tie for steepest, D8 breaks the tie in the same order Esri's Flow Direction does (west, north, south, east, then the diagonals), and on a 30 m integer DEM the D8 accumulation matched Esri's exactly on 85 percent of cells and within 5 percent on 91 percent; the remainder is flats, where the exit a flat drains to is a matter of convention. If you need results identical to an Esri workflow, supply your Esri flow-accumulation raster (see the optional parameters) and the tool will use it directly.
Flow routing methods. D8 (the default; O'Callaghan and Mark 1984) sends all of a cell's water to its single steepest lower neighbor: right in channels, wrong on convex ground, where water actually spreads, so a cell on a hillside receives only the one thread of cells that happens to point at it. D-Infinity (Tarboton 1997) fits eight triangular facets around the cell, takes the steepest facet's direction as a continuous angle, and splits the water between the two neighbors that bracket it in proportion to the angle, so the flow spreads only as much as the terrain says. MFD (Quinn et al. 1991, with the adaptive partition exponent of Qin et al. 2007 that Esri's MFD option also implements) sends a share to every lower neighbor, weighted by the slope toward it raised to an exponent that rises with the local steepness, and by the contour length toward that neighbor; it disperses more than D-Infinity. Under D-Infinity and MFD the accumulation is fractional (a cell's area is shared among its receivers), and the specific catchment area is the same formula for all three: (accumulation + 1) x cell size. The divisor is the width of the cell whose value is being computed, not the number of cells it sends water to (Tarboton 1997: a = A/L with L the pixel width); the spreading is already expressed in the smaller shares each downslope cell receives. Sorensen et al. (2006) found no single routing method best for every field variable; D8 is the convention of most published TWI recipes.

dialogReference.para: The elevation raster (DEM) to compute the Topographic Wetness Index from. It must be single band. Both projected and geographic (latitude/longitude) coordinate systems are supported; on a geographic DEM the ground cell size and slope are computed per row on the spheroid.
Unless you supply a flow-accumulation raster below, this DEM is filled and flow-routed internally. The slope term always comes from this original (unfilled) DEM.

The output floating-point TWI raster: ln( specific catchment area / (tan(slope) + epsilon) ). Higher values are wetter (large upslope area and/or gentle slope); lower values are drier (ridges, steep slopes). NoData outside the valid DEM area. A suggested name is filled in from the input, and a dry-to-wet color ramp is applied. The output carries statistics and a histogram.

How to measure the ground distances used in the slope calculation, for projected DEMs only (this control is disabled for geographic DEMs, which are always computed geodesically on the spheroid, per row).

Planar (the default) measures slope in the projected coordinate system's plane, using the raster's cell size directly. This matches Esri's Slope tool with the Planar method and is the right choice for nearly all projected DEMs.

Geodesic instead uses true ground distances between cell centers (obtained by unprojecting them onto the datum's spheroid), correcting for the projection's scale distortion. On typical low-distortion projections (UTM, State Plane) it is essentially identical to Planar; it becomes meaningful only for large-extent or highly distorted projections (for example, Web Mercator spanning a wide range of latitudes). This is a true-ground-distance correction and is not intended to reproduce Esri's proprietary geocentric Geodesic method exactly.

The DEM's elevation units, Meters or Feet. Filled in and locked automatically when the DEM defines a vertical coordinate system; you are only asked to choose when the DEM does not say. Elevation is converted internally so that the vertical and horizontal units match, giving a correct (dimensionless) slope gradient regardless of whether the DEM is in meters or feet.

A small positive constant added to the slope gradient (the tangent of the slope angle) before dividing, so that perfectly flat cells (slope 0) do not cause a divide-by-zero. The default, 0.0001, is the value used in common TWI recipes. A flat cell then receives a high TWI (very wet), which is the intended behavior. Larger values pull very flat cells toward lower TWI; smaller values push them higher.

param.name: flow_method
param.displayname: Flow routing method (when the tool computes the flow accumulation)

dialogReference.para: How water is routed from each cell of the filled surface when the tool computes the flow accumulation itself. D8 (the default): all of a cell's water goes to its single steepest lower neighbor; the convention of most TWI recipes and of Esri's default. MFD: every lower neighbor receives a share, weighted by slope raised to an adaptive exponent (Qin et al. 2007) and by contour length; the most dispersive choice. DINF (D-Infinity, Tarboton 1997): the two neighbors that bracket the steepest facet direction share the water in proportion to the angle; spreads flow on convex ground without the lateral dispersion of MFD.

Under MFD and D-Infinity the accumulation is fractional and the specific catchment area is still (accumulation + 1) x cell size. Disabled when you supply your own flow-accumulation raster, since the routing is then already done.

Optional. A depression-filled (hydrologically conditioned) version of the input DEM to use as the flow-routing surface, so the tool skips its own fill step. It must share the input DEM's grid (same extent, cell size, and alignment). The slope term still comes from the original DEM, not this one. Ignored if you also supply a flow-accumulation raster below.

Optional. A pre-computed flow-accumulation raster (upstream cell count, as produced by Esri's Flow Accumulation or by this tool). If supplied, the tool skips filling, flow direction, and accumulation entirely and uses this raster's values directly - the fastest path, and the way to reproduce an Esri D8 workflow exactly. It must share the input DEM's grid.

Optional. If you set a path here, the depression-filled DEM the tool computes is saved to it, for reuse or inspection. This option is available only when the tool actually computes the fill - it is disabled if you supply your own filled DEM or a flow-accumulation raster.

Optional. If you set a path here, the flow-accumulation raster the tool computes (upslope area in cells, excluding the cell itself; fractional under MFD and D-Infinity) is saved to it, for reuse or inspection. This option is available only when the tool actually computes accumulation - it is disabled if you supply your own flow-accumulation raster.

scriptExample.title: Topographic Wetness Index example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Compute TWI from a DEM, letting the tool fill and flow-route internally, and saving the intermediate flow accumulation.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages arcpy.jenness.TopographicWetnessIndex( in_raster="dem.tif", out_raster="dem_TWI.tif", slope_method="Planar", elev_units="Meters", slope_epsilon=0.0001, flow_method="D8 (single flow direction)", # or "MFD (multiple flow direction; Qin et al. 2007)" / "DINF (D-Infinity; Tarboton 1997)" out_flow_accumulation="dem_flowacc.tif")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Topographic Wetness Index (TWI / CTI) = ln(specific catchment area / (tan(slope) + epsilon)) from a DEM, with sink filling, flow direction (D8, MFD or D-Infinity) and flow accumulation computed internally (no Spatial Analyst); high values mark wet valley bottoms and convergence zones.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Computes the per-cell Topographic Wetness Index (also called the Compound Topographic Index), ln( specific catchment area / (tan(slope) + epsilon) ), after Beven and Kirkby (1979). The specific catchment area is (flow accumulation + 1) times the cell size, taking each cell's own edge as the unit contour length; the +1 includes the cell itself and keeps the logarithm defined, and a small epsilon (default 0.0001) added to the slope gradient avoids division by zero on flats. Slope is Horn's gradient of the original (unfilled) DEM - planar on projected DEMs, or optionally geodesic, and always geodesic per row on geographic DEMs. Depression filling (priority-flood; Barnes, Lehman and Mulla 2014), flow direction by D8 (O'Callaghan and Mark 1984), MFD (Quinn et al. 1991; Qin et al. 2007) or D-Infinity (Tarboton 1997), and flow accumulation are computed internally with numpy - no Spatial Analyst extension - and match Esri's Fill, Flow Direction, and Flow Accumulation closely (fill identically; D8 and D-Infinity to more than 99.7 percent of cells on a projected DEM, the remainder flat-area tie-breaking; MFD within 5 percent on about 83 percent of cells). Users may supply a pre-filled DEM and/or a flow-accumulation raster to skip those steps (or to reproduce an Esri workflow exactly), and may save the computed filled DEM and flow accumulation. Output carries statistics, a histogram, and a dry-to-wet color ramp.
